The edge count is fixed by m while which pairs get joined is random." width="100%"} Creates a graph with `n` nodes and exactly `m` randomly placed edges. This model is useful for generating random graphs with a fixed number of edges. The method adds `n` new, unlabelled nodes, lists every possible edge among them, shuffles that list, and keeps the first `m`. Every set of `m` distinct edges is equally likely. In an undirected graph the candidates are the `n(n - 1) / 2` unordered pairs; in a directed graph they are the `n(n - 1)` ordered pairs, so `u -> v` and `v -> u` are separate candidates. Self-loops and duplicate edges are never created. Existing nodes are left untouched and never connected to the new ones. G(n, m) is the fixed-size counterpart of `add_gnp_graph()`. Use it when the exact edge count matters, for example: - building a random null model with the same number of nodes and edges as an observed network - benchmarking algorithms at a precise size or density - comparing several random graphs that differ only in how their edges are placed The full list of candidate pairs is built in memory, so time and memory grow as `n^2` regardless of `m=`. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [n]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Number of nodes to add. The new nodes have no labels and get the next available node IDs. [m]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Exact number of edges to create among the new nodes. Must not exceed the number of possible pairs: `n(n - 1) / 2` for undirected graphs or `n(n - 1)` for directed ones. Larger values raise a `ValueError`. [directed]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[bool]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Leave as `None` (default) to generate edges according to the graph's own directedness. Passing the graph's own setting (`graph.is_directed()`) does the same thing. Passing a value that differs from it generates the edges as if the graph had that directedness: `directed=True` on an undirected graph considers both orientations of each pair (so a pair can get two parallel edges), and `directed=False` on a directed graph considers each pair once and stores the edge in one direction. [seed]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Integer seed for the random number generator. The same `seed=` with the same `n=` and `m=` always picks the same edges. If `None` (default), the result differs on every call. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Self for method chaining. The graph is modified in place. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `m=` is larger than the number of possible edges among `n=` nodes. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} Unlike `add_gnp_graph()`, which samples edges probabilistically, this fixes the exact number of edges -- `m=100` always produces exactly `100` edges, regardless of seed: ::: {#01045cd9 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_gnm_graph(n=50, m=100, seed=23) ) graph.count_nodes(), graph.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (50, 100) ``` ::: ::: Changing `seed=` keeps the edge count but changes which pairs are joined. Both of these graphs have four edges, placed differently: ::: {#9959e645 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} first = ec.Graph().add_gnm_graph(n=6, m=4, seed=1) second = ec.Graph().add_gnm_graph(n=6, m=4, seed=2) first.get_edges_str_repr(), second.get_edges_str_repr() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (['1--3', '1--5', '4--6', '1--2'], ['1--3', '1--6', '1--5', '3--4']) ``` ::: ::: In a directed graph the two orientations of a pair are separate candidates, so four nodes can hold up to `4 * 3 = 12` edges. Asking for all of them gives a complete directed graph: ::: {#99c6b072 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} directed = ec.Graph(directed=True).add_gnm_graph(n=4, m=12) directed.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` 12 ``` ::: :::
